mainTopic: Conditional oaths on two loaves, the proof that a condition fulfilled by mistake does not count, and אבימי's test of עיפא on when a repeated oath takes effect.
overview: The גמרא finishes its cases of a שבועה with a condition, like 'I will not eat this loaf if I eat that loaf.' When both loaves are eaten on purpose, the order matters. If he ate the forbidden loaf first, the warning he got was only a התראת ספק, and that depends on the dispute between רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש. In a two-way oath, where each loaf is the condition for the other, he is liable only if he knowingly fulfilled the condition that made the other loaf forbidden. רב מרי supports this from the משנה in נדרים about mistaken vows, together with a ברייתא saying mistaken oaths are released too. Then the גמרא tells how אבימי tested his brother עיפא with three questions about repeated oaths, and corrected all three answers. An oath about the past is a new lie each time. A second oath only takes effect if it forbids something new. At the end, אביי starts showing that עיפא's 'ten then nine' answer can sometimes be right, using a case of רבה about figs and grapes that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Both loaves eaten on purpose: condition loaf first, then the forbidden loaf
steps.stepSummary: If he ate both loaves במזיד, eating the condition loaf first and then the forbidden loaf, he is liable to מלקות.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he ate both on purpose, first the condition loaf and then the forbidden loaf, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues its list of cases for a one-way conditional oath. Here he ate both loaves on purpose, and the condition loaf came first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once he eats the condition loaf, the oath takes hold and the second loaf is clearly forbidden. When he is warned before eating it, the warning is certain, so he gets מלקות.

keyTerms.meaning: On purpose, knowing it is forbidden
His condition: the loaf whose eating triggers the oath
His forbidden item: the loaf the oath forbids
He becomes liable

phrases.english: If both of them were eaten intentionally –
if he ate the loaf of his condition
phrases.notes: This is the loaf in the 'if I eat this' part of his oath.

phrases.english: and then ate the forbidden loaf, he is liable;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of cases from the earlier part of the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Condition loaf first, then the forbidden loaf, both on purpose: liable to מלקות.

steps.title: Forbidden loaf eaten first: depends on the dispute about an uncertain warning
steps.stepSummary: If he ate the forbidden loaf first and the condition loaf afterward, liability depends on the dispute between רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש about התראת ספק.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he ate the forbidden loaf first and then the condition loaf, this depends on the argument between רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש. The one who says an uncertain warning counts as a warning holds he is liable. The one who says it does not count holds he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reverses the order. He eats the forbidden loaf first and only afterward eats the condition loaf.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When he was warned before eating the first loaf, it was not yet forbidden. It would only become forbidden if he later ate the condition loaf, so the warning was uncertain. Whether he gets מלקות depends on whether such a warning counts.

keyTerms.meaning: A dispute
A warning given before a sin, needed for מלקות
An uncertain warning, when it is not yet clear the act will turn out forbidden
According to the one who says

steps.confusionAlert: Even though the forbidden loaf is eaten first, it can still turn out forbidden, because the oath is decided once he eats the condition loaf. The question is only about the warning, not whether a sin happened.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the order of eating can decide whether the classic dispute about התראת ספק comes into play.

phrases.english: If he ate the forbidden loaf
and then ate the loaf of his condition,
it is the dispute of Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish –

phrases.aramaic: לְמַאן דְּאָמַר הַתְרָאַת סָפֵק שְׁמָהּ הַתְרָאָה, חַיָּיב;
phrases.english: according to the one who says an uncertain warning is called a warning, he is liable;

phrases.aramaic: לְמַאן דְּאָמַר לָאו שְׁמָהּ הַתְרָאָה, פָּטוּר.
phrases.english: according to the one who says it is not called a warning, he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The reverse order of the case in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Forbidden loaf first: liable if התראת ספק counts as a warning, exempt if it does not.

steps.title: Each loaf conditional on the other: aware of each loaf's own oath, unaware of its effect on the other
steps.stepSummary: In a two-way oath, if he ate each loaf knowing its own oath but not realizing he was making the other loaf forbidden, he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he made them depend on each other ('I will not eat this if I eat that,' and 'I will not eat that if I eat this'), and he ate each one aware of its own oath but unaware that it made the other forbidden, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new kind of case, where each loaf is both a condition and a forbidden loaf. Its first case: he knows about each loaf's own oath but not about its effect on the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each loaf is forbidden only once the other loaf is eaten as a condition. Here each condition was fulfilled by mistake, because he did not know he was making the other loaf forbidden. Since the conditions were met only by mistake, he is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: He made them depend on each other
Knowing about this loaf's own oath
Not realizing it affects the other loaf
Exempt

steps.confusionAlert: 'On purpose regarding itself' sounds like the worse case, but he is exempt. What matters is whether he knowingly fulfilled the condition that makes the other loaf forbidden.

phrases.english: If he made them depend on each other –
'I will not eat this if I eat that,'
'I will not eat that if I eat this';
phrases.notes: The Hebrew is the same words twice. The second time, the two loaves switch places.

phrases.english: and he ate this one knowing about its own oath
but unaware regarding the other,
phrases.notes: He forgot that eating this loaf makes the other loaf forbidden.

phrases.english: and that one knowing about its own oath
but unaware regarding the other – he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from a one-way condition to a two-way condition.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two-way oath, each loaf eaten aware of its own oath but unaware of its effect on the other: exempt.

steps.title: Each loaf conditional on the other: unaware of each loaf's own oath, aware of its effect on the other
steps.stepSummary: If he ate each loaf forgetting its own oath but knowing he was making the other forbidden, he is liable to קרבנות.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he ate this one unaware of its own oath but aware regarding the other, and that one the same way, he is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא flips the previous case. Now he knowingly fulfills each condition but forgets that the loaf he is eating is itself forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because each condition was fulfilled knowingly, both oaths take effect. He then ate each forbidden loaf בשוגג, so he is liable to a קרבן for unknowingly breaking his oath.

keyTerms.meaning: Unaware of this loaf's own oath
Aware that he is making the other loaf forbidden
Liable (here: to a קרבן)

phrases.english: If he ate this one unaware of its own oath
but aware regarding the other,
and that one unaware of its own oath
but aware regarding the other – he is liable.
phrases.notes: Since he sinned by mistake, 'liable' here means bringing a קרבן, not מלקות.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The mirror image of step 3, with the opposite result.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two-way oath, each condition fulfilled knowingly but each loaf eaten by mistake: liable to a קרבן.

steps.title: Each loaf conditional on the other: both eaten by mistake
steps.stepSummary: If both loaves were eaten בשוגג in every way, he is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he ate both of them by mistake, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the next two-way case, where he was unaware of everything. The last case, where both loaves are eaten on purpose, comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Neither condition was fulfilled knowingly, so neither oath ever took effect. With no oath in force, eating the loaves carries no liability.

keyTerms.meaning: By mistake, without knowing

steps.whatToRemember: In a two-way oath, liability depends on whether he knew he was fulfilling the condition that forbids the other loaf. Knowing the condition makes the oaths take effect (step 4: liable). Being unaware of the condition means the oaths never take effect (steps 3 and 5: exempt). The next step covers the case where he ate both on purpose.

phrases.english: If both of them were eaten unwittingly – he is exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The third case in the two-way list, after steps 3 and 4. The fully intentional case follows in step 6.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: When both loaves are eaten by mistake, no condition was knowingly fulfilled, so he is exempt.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two-way oath, both loaves eaten completely by mistake: exempt, since neither condition was knowingly fulfilled.

steps.title: Two-way oath with both loaves eaten on purpose
steps.stepSummary: In the two-way oath, if he ate both loaves במזיד, he is liable for the second loaf. For the first loaf, the outcome depends on the רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש dispute about התראת ספק.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he ate both of them on purpose: for the second one he is liable. For the first one, it depends on the argument between רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives the last case of the two-way oath, where each loaf is both the condition and the forbidden loaf. Here he ate both loaves on purpose.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When he eats the second loaf, the first is already eaten, so the second is definitely forbidden. That means the warning he received was certain, and he gets מלקות. When he ate the first loaf, nobody knew yet whether he would ever eat the second, so the first loaf was only possibly forbidden. Any warning at that point was a התראת ספק, which is exactly what רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש argue about.

keyTerms.meaning: Both of them (both loaves)
For the second one
For the first one
A dispute, an argument between Sages

steps.confusionAlert: In a two-way oath each loaf is both a condition and a forbidden loaf. 'First' and 'second' here mean the order he ate them in, not which loaf was named first in the oath.

phrases.english: If he ate both of them intentionally,
for the second one he is liable,
for the first one, it is the dispute
phrases.notes: This is the same argument as in Step 2: whether a warning about something only possibly forbidden counts.

phrases.english: of Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבא's set of two-way oath cases by addressing the fully intentional case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both loaves eaten במזיד: liable to מלקות for the second loaf; for the first, it depends on the התראת ספק dispute.

steps.title: רב מרי brings a supporting משנה about four kinds of vows
steps.stepSummary: רב מרי says there is a משנה that supports רבא: the Sages released four kinds of vows, including mistaken vows.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מרי said: we have also learned this in a משנה. The Sages released four kinds of vows: vows of urging, vows of exaggeration, mistaken vows, and vows blocked by circumstances beyond one's control.
steps.whatsHappening: רב מרי starts a proof for רבא's idea that a condition fulfilled by mistake does not trigger the oath. Here he only lays out the משנה, which sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה lists four kinds of vows that are not binding at all, with no need to go to a חכם. The one that matters for our proof is נדרי שגגות, mistaken vows. The משנה explains that one in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: We too have also learned this (in a משנה), introducing support
Vows of urging, said to pressure someone in a deal
Vows of exaggeration, plainly overstated
Mistaken vows, made on a wrong assumption or broken without awareness
Vows that cannot be kept because of circumstances beyond one's control

phrases.english: Rav Mari said:
We too have also learned this:
phrases.notes: He means רבא's rule from Steps 3 and 5, that a condition fulfilled by mistake does not trigger the oath.

phrases.english: Four kinds of vows the Sages released:
phrases.notes: This is the משנה in נדרים 20b.

phrases.english: vows of urging, vows of exaggeration,
mistaken vows, and vows blocked by circumstances beyond one's control.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב מָרִי, אַף אֲנַן נָמֵי תְּנֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a proof supporting רבא's rulings that eating the condition loaf בשוגג does not activate the oath.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's rule that fulfilling the condition of an oath unknowingly leaves him exempt.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in נדרים listing four kinds of vows the Sages released, including נדרי שגגות.

steps.title: The cases of mistaken vows, and a ברייתא that applies them to oaths
steps.stepSummary: The משנה explains mistaken vows, including one where the person forgot and did the very thing he vowed about. A ברייתא adds that mistaken oaths are released just like mistaken vows.
steps.simpleTranslation: How do mistaken vows work? Someone says, 'קונם, if I ate or if I drank,' and then remembers that he did eat and drink. Or he says, 'קונם, if I will eat or drink,' and then forgets and eats and drinks. In both cases the item is permitted. A ברייתא taught on this: just as mistaken vows are released, mistaken oaths are released too.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה defines mistaken vows with two cases. A ברייתא then extends the rule from vows to oaths.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second case is the important one. He made a conditional vow about future eating, then forgot and fulfilled the condition, and the item stays permitted. The ברייתא says the same thing works for שבועות. That brings the rule into our case of a conditional oath on loaves.

keyTerms.meaning: A vow word meaning 'forbidden to me like a קרבן'
And he remembered (afterward)
He forgot
And a ברייתא taught about it
Mistaken oaths

phrases.english: Mistaken vows, how so?
"Konam, if I ate and if I drank,"
phrases.notes: He made some item forbidden to himself on the condition that he had already eaten or drunk.

phrases.english: and he remembered that he did eat and drink;
"if I will eat, if I will drink,"
and he forgot and ate and drank, it is permitted.
And a ברייתא taught about it:
Just as mistaken vows are released,
so too mistaken oaths are released.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the נדרי שגגות category from the משנה and extends it to oaths through a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: That a condition fulfilled while forgetting leaves the vow or oath without effect.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's case of 'שכח ואכל ושתה – מותר' plus the ברייתא equating mistaken oaths with mistaken vows.

steps.title: Mistaken oaths must mean our case, so the proof stands
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what a 'mistaken oath' would look like. It must be a case like ours, where the condition was fulfilled unknowingly, so רבא's ruling is supported.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is a mistaken oath? Isn't it a case just like this one? Learn from it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes רב מרי's proof. It applies the ברייתא's 'mistaken oaths' to a conditional oath whose condition was fulfilled without awareness, and concludes that רבא is supported.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question 'היכי דמי' is rhetorical. The only sensible picture of a mistaken oath is like the משנה's vow case: he forgot and fulfilled the condition. That is exactly רבא's case of eating the condition loaf בשוגג, so the oath does not take effect and he is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: What are the circumstances? What does it look like?
Is it not like this case? (rhetorical: it must be)
Learn from it, the proof is accepted

steps.whatToRemember: Fulfilling the condition of a conditional oath without realizing it is a שבועת שגגות. The oath does not take effect, as רבא ruled, and רב מרי proves it from the משנה in נדרים.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that an oath's condition only counts when it is fulfilled knowingly. That is the basis for the exemptions in רבא's two-loaf cases.

phrases.english: Mistaken oaths, what are the circumstances?
Is it not a case like this one?
phrases.notes: 'This one' means רבא's case: a conditional oath where he ate the condition loaf without realizing it.

phrases.english: Learn from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the ברייתא's term 'mistaken oaths' to רבא's case and closes the proof.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A conditional oath whose condition was fulfilled unknowingly is a mistaken oath and is not binding, which confirms רבא's ruling.

steps.title: אבימי tests his brother with two oaths about the past
steps.stepSummary: עיפא learned שבועות in רבה's yeshiva. His brother אבימי asks him: if someone swore twice, 'I did not eat,' what is the law?
steps.simpleTranslation: עיפא learned מסכת שבועות in רבה's yeshiva. His brother אבימי met him and asked: if a person says 'I swear I did not eat,' and then again 'I swear I did not eat,' what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story. אבימי tests his brother's knowledge with a question about two identical oaths about the past.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both oaths talk about something that already happened. The question is whether he is punished once or twice, if in fact he did eat.

keyTerms.meaning: A Sage, the brother of אבימי, who learned in רבה's yeshiva
עיפא's brother, who tests him here
'I swear I did not eat': an oath about the past
What is the law?

phrases.english: Eifa learned Shevuot in the academy of Rabba.
His brother Avimi met him,
he said to him:
'On my oath I did not eat,'
'On my oath I did not eat,' what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the proof for רבא in step 9.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is a person who swears the same false oath about the past twice liable once or twice?

steps.title: עיפא answers that he is liable only once
steps.stepSummary: עיפא says the person is liable only one time.
steps.simpleTranslation: עיפא said to him: he is liable only once.
steps.whatsHappening: עיפא gives his answer: two oaths, but only one punishment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: עיפא seems to treat the second oath like a repeated future oath. A repeated future oath does not take effect, because the first oath already covers it.

keyTerms.meaning: He is liable only once

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב אֶלָּא אַחַת.
phrases.english: He said to him: He is liable only once.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אבימי's question.

steps.title: אבימי: each past oath is its own lie
steps.stepSummary: אבימי says עיפא is mistaken. Each oath about the past is a separate false oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: אבימי said: You are mixed up! Each time, a false oath came out of his mouth.
steps.whatsHappening: אבימי rejects עיפא's answer and explains why.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a future oath, the question is whether the second oath can take hold at all. An oath about the past is simply true or false the moment it is said. So each time he said it, he swore falsely, and he is liable twice.

keyTerms.meaning: You are mixed up / you have made a mistake
A false oath came out (of his mouth)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up past and future oaths. A second future oath on the same thing does not take effect. But every false oath about the past is its own new sin.

phrases.english: He said to him: You have confused the issue,
a false oath was issued!
phrases.notes: He means it happened each time. Every oath was a fresh lie, so each one counts.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges עיפא's answer.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Fully rejects עיפא's ruling for past oaths.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: עיפא applied the 'second oath doesn't take effect' idea to past oaths. With past oaths, each statement is a separate lie.

steps.title: Second question: nine, then ten
steps.stepSummary: אבימי asks: if one swore not to eat nine, and then swore not to eat ten, what is the law?
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone said: 'I swear I will not eat nine,' and 'I swear I will not eat ten,' what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: אבימי asks a new question. This time the oaths are about the future, and the second one covers a bigger amount.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first oath forbids nine pieces. The second oath forbids ten pieces. The question is whether the second oath adds anything.

keyTerms.meaning: 'I swear I will not eat': an oath about the future
Nine and ten (pieces)

phrases.english: 'On my oath I will not eat
nine and ten,' what is the law?
phrases.notes: These are two separate oaths, first about nine pieces and then about ten. The word 'pieces' is assumed.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁלֹּא אוֹכַל תֵּשַׁע וְעֶשֶׂר מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new test question from אבימי.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does an oath forbidding ten take effect after an oath forbidding nine?

steps.title: עיפא: liable for each oath
steps.stepSummary: עיפא answers that he is liable for each and every oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: He is liable for each and every one.
steps.whatsHappening: עיפא says both oaths count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: עיפא's reasoning seems to be that the second oath covers more (ten instead of nine). So it adds something new and should take effect.

keyTerms.meaning: Liable for each and every one

phrases.english: He is liable for each and every one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the nine-then-ten question.

steps.title: אבימי: ten is already forbidden by nine
steps.stepSummary: אבימי says: if he may not eat nine, he certainly may not eat ten. So the second oath has nothing new to forbid.
steps.simpleTranslation: You are mixed up! If he can't eat nine, he can't eat ten.
steps.whatsHappening: אבימי rejects עיפא's answer again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eating ten always includes eating nine, and nine is already forbidden by the first oath. An oath cannot take effect on something that is already forbidden by an oath, so the 'ten' oath does nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: If he may not eat nine

phrases.english: He said to him: You have confused the issue,
if he may not eat nine,
he may not eat ten!
phrases.notes: You can't eat ten without eating nine first, so the 'ten' oath forbids nothing new.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי תֵּשַׁע לָא אָכֵיל, עֶשֶׂר לָא אָכֵיל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges עיפא's answer to the second question.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ten-oath only forbids something that is already forbidden by the nine-oath.

steps.title: Third question: ten, then nine
steps.stepSummary: אבימי flips the order: an oath not to eat ten, and then an oath not to eat nine. What is the law?
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone said: 'I swear I will not eat ten,' and 'I swear I will not eat nine,' what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: אבימי asks the same case, but with the order reversed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the bigger amount comes first and the smaller amount comes second. The question is whether the second oath adds anything this time.

keyTerms.meaning: Ten and nine (pieces)

phrases.english: 'On my oath I will not eat
ten and nine,' what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁבוּעָה שֶׁלֹּא אוֹכַל עֶשֶׂר וָתֵשַׁע מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The reverse of the previous case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does an oath forbidding nine take effect after an oath forbidding ten?

steps.title: עיפא: liable only once
steps.stepSummary: עיפא answers that he is liable only once.
steps.simpleTranslation: He is liable only once.
steps.whatsHappening: עיפא says only one oath counts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: עיפא seems to think the 'nine' oath is already included inside the 'ten' oath, so it adds nothing.

phrases.english: He is liable only once.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the ten-then-nine question.

steps.title: אבימי: the first oath still allowed nine
steps.stepSummary: אבימי says the 'ten' oath only forbids eating ten. Eating nine was still allowed, so the second oath does take effect on nine.
steps.simpleTranslation: You are mixed up! It is ten that he may not eat, but nine he may still eat.
steps.whatsHappening: אבימי rejects עיפא's answer for the third time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An oath against eating ten is only broken by eating all ten. Eating nine was still allowed under the first oath. So the second oath forbids something new, and it takes effect.

keyTerms.meaning: But nine, at least, he may eat

steps.whatToRemember: An oath only takes effect if it forbids something that was not already forbidden. Nine then ten: the second oath does nothing. Ten then nine: the second oath works. Two oaths about the past: each one is a separate lie.

phrases.english: He said to him: You have confused the issue,
it is ten that he may not eat,
but nine, at least, he may eat!

steps.triggerLanguage: עֶשֶׂר הוּא דְּלָא אָכֵיל, הָא תֵּשַׁע מִיהָא אָכֵיל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges עיפא's answer to the third question.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The first oath did not forbid nine, so the second oath has something new to forbid.

steps.title: אביי: sometimes עיפא's answer is right
steps.stepSummary: אביי says there are cases where עיפא's ruling (ten then nine: liable only once) really is true, like a case of רבה.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Sometimes you can find a case where עיפא's ruling fits, like the ruling of the Master.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי defends עיפא. He sets up a proof that will come from רבה's case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי does not say אבימי was wrong in general. He says there is a specific kind of case where עיפא's answer of 'only once' holds.

keyTerms.meaning: Sometimes you can find it
Like the Master (here meaning רבה)

phrases.english: Abaye said:
There are times when you find it,
this ruling of Eifa, as the Master said.
phrases.notes: He means עיפא's last answer, that 'ten then nine' makes him liable only once. 'The Master' is רבה, as the next line shows.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Partly saves עיפא's rejected answer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In certain cases, an oath on a big thing followed by an oath on a smaller part of it brings only one liability.

steps.title: רבה's case: figs and grapes, then figs
steps.stepSummary: אביי brings רבה's case: an oath not to eat figs and grapes, and then an oath not to eat figs.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבה said: one who says, 'I swear I will not eat figs and grapes,' and then says, 'I swear I will not eat figs'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins quoting רבה's case as אביי's source. רבה's ruling on it comes in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This matches 'ten then nine.' The first oath covers a bigger set (figs and grapes together), and the second covers only part of it (figs). The ruling that follows will show how עיפא's 'only once' can be true here.

keyTerms.meaning: Figs and grapes
And then he said again

phrases.english: As Rabba says:
'On my oath I will not eat figs and grapes,'
phrases.notes: He means eating both together, just like the 'ten' oath.

phrases.english: and then says:
'On my oath I will not eat figs';

steps.raayaObject: אביי's claim that עיפא's 'ten then nine' ruling sometimes applies.
